traveler: Taj al-Din Ali ibn Muhammad Ibn al-Durayhim al-Mawsili
title: Key to the Treasures: Mosul, Cairo, and the Cipher Book That Went Missing Twice
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Basra, the first book of enciphered words
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi lived c. 718-786 and the Kitab al-Mu'amma is undated within his career. The pin marks the original garrison site of Basra near al-Zubayr, some fifteen kilometres southwest of the modern city, which only moved to the Shatt al-Arab in the late 900s. His birthplace is disputed between Oman and Basra
stops.campa: In the garrison city at the edge of the marshes, al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi writes a book called Kitab al-Mu'amma, on enciphered messages, and what he does in it is count. He is the maker of the first Arabic dictionary and a measurer of poetic meter, and he handles the alphabet as a stock of parts: how many words a root can yield, how many arrangements a pattern permits. The counting passes down through the grammarians who come after him, and five and a half centuries later a scholar of Mosul will be praised for discourse on letters and their properties. The cipher book itself does not survive, and no later writer quotes a line of it.
suggested_refs: Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi's Kitab al-Mu'amma, the lost first Arabic book on ciphers

stops.name: Baghdad, the treatise on deciphering
stops.date_confidence: attested to al-Kindi's Baghdad career; the Risala fi Istikhraj al-Kutub al-Mu'ammah carries no composition date and the year here is the pin already used in the corpus for it
stops.campa: Al-Kindi writes the Risala fi Istikhraj al-Kutub al-Mu'ammah and sets down what nobody has written before: take a long stretch of ordinary Arabic, count how often each letter falls, lay the tally against the coded text, and let the commonest stand for the commonest. Frequency analysis begins on this page. Ibn Adlan in Cairo and Ibn al-Durayhim after him will work from the method rather than from the book, which drops out of circulation for eleven hundred years.
suggested_refs: Al-Kindi, Risala fi Istikhraj al-Kutub al-Mu'ammah, the founding treatise of cryptanalysis

stops.name: Baghdad, the philosopher dies and the papers scatter
stops.date_confidence: attested to c. 873 (256 AH); the day and month are not recorded, and the fate of his personal papers is inference rather than record
stops.campa: Al-Kindi dies in Baghdad in his seventies. Ibn al-Nadim will credit him with at least two hundred and sixty works, on optics, medicine, music, metallurgy, the tempering of swords, and most of them are already sliding out of the record. More than a decade before the end, al-Mutawakkil's men had beaten him and carried off his library, and then returned it. In 1258 the Mongols take the city and its libraries go into the Tigris, and whatever remained of his papers there goes with them, if the chroniclers are telling the truth.
suggested_refs: Ibn al-Nadim's Fihrist and its list of al-Kindi's works

stops.name: Mosul, the second cryptanalyst is born
stops.date_confidence: attested to 583 AH / 1187 by Arabic Wikipedia; the month is not given. The pin is the Great Mosque of al-Nuri, the city's congregational mosque, not a documented birth site
stops.campa: Ali ibn Adlan al-Mawsili is born in Mosul, in a city whose congregational mosque and leaning minaret are barely fifteen years old, raised by Nur al-Din Zangi in 1172. He studies language and literature with the Mukabbari grammarians and takes up cryptanalysis as one puzzle among the puzzles a man of letters keeps. A hundred and twenty-five years later another boy will be born into this same city and this same combination of interests, and no source records that he ever hears Ibn Adlan's name at home.
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of al-Nuri and the al-Hadba minaret, built 1172-73

stops.name: Aleppo, one stop on the scholar's circuit
stops.date_confidence: attested only as a stop in Arabic Wikipedia's itinerary for Ibn Adlan, with no year, no duration and no named patron. The date is an arbitrary placement inside his adult life and should not be read as evidence
stops.campa: Ibn Adlan leaves Mosul for Aleppo, one stop on a circuit that thirteenth-century Syria and Iraq make routine: a grammarian moves from patron to patron, city to city, wherever a stipend or a teaching post opens. Above the town stands the citadel on its mound, the strongest fortress in Syria, garrisoned and busy. What he does here, how long he stays, whose household he serves, the sources consulted for this account do not say. Only the fact of the stop survives, one line in an itinerary that ends in Cairo.
suggested_refs: The Citadel of Aleppo in the Ayyubid period

stops.name: Damascus, the stop before Egypt
stops.date_confidence: attested as a stop only, undated in Arabic Wikipedia; the year is an arbitrary placement. The pin is the canonical Damascus pin used elsewhere in the corpus and marks the Umayyad Mosque quarter approximately
stops.campa: Damascus is the stop before Egypt. Ibn Adlan passes through a city where the Umayyad Mosque has by now held six hundred years of continuous prayer, and where a man building a name in language and letters can find an audience for it in an afternoon. What work he does here the sources consulted do not specify, and there is nothing to guess with. The Mamluk capital pays better and keeps better records; the biographers pick him up again only once he has arrived there.
suggested_refs: The Umayyad Mosque of Damascus as a teaching centre in the thirteenth century

stops.name: Cairo, how much ciphertext is enough
stops.date_confidence: attested to Ibn Adlan's lifetime, 1187 to 1268; his treatise is not dated within it. The ninety-character minimum is reported in the corpus and in secondary cryptology history rather than read off the manuscript
stops.campa: Ibn Adlan settles in Cairo, teaches Arabic, and asks the question al-Kindi left open: counting works, but on how much text? He sets out twenty groups of rules, handles ciphers written without spaces between the words, and fixes a minimum sample near ninety characters, below which the frequencies simply lie. His manual is practical throughout, a set of procedures for texts that come across a desk rather than an argument about method. Where he got the figure of ninety the treatise does not explain.
stops.quote: Unlike the cryptological treatises of Al-Kindi before him and later Ibn al-Durayhim (c. 1312-1361), which provide theoretical background on cryptography including systematic explanations on types of ciphers, Ibn 'Adlan's On Cryptanalysis focuses on the practical matters and specific methods in breaking encrypted texts of his time.
suggested_refs: Ibn Adlan's On Cryptanalysis and its minimum-sample rule

stops.name: Cairo, the chain waits forty-four years
stops.date_confidence: attested to 666 AH / 1268 by Arabic Wikipedia; no day or month, and no burial place recorded in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Ibn Adlan dies in Cairo in 666 of the Hijra, a Mosul man ending in Egypt, and the biographers will have occasion to write that sentence again. He leaves a short practical manual rather than a system: the work of someone who broke ciphers and set down what worked, teaching Arabic at the Salihiyya mosque to pay for the time it took. Where he is buried the sources consulted do not say. Nor do they say who, if anyone, was reading the manual in the forty-four years before the next man in this line is born.
suggested_refs: The Salihiyya mosque-madrasa of Cairo, where Ibn Adlan taught

stops.name: Mosul, born in Sha'ban of the year 712
stops.date_confidence: attested to Sha'ban 712 AH by Arabic Wikipedia, which falls in about December 1312; English Wikipedia gives the year 1312 alone with no month. The pin is the city's congregational mosque, not a documented birth site, and the nisba al-Mawsili is the only evidence that Mosul is the birthplace at all
stops.campa: A son is born in Mosul in Sha'ban of the year 712, into the Taghlib and the Shafi'i school: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Aziz ibn Futuh ibn Ibrahim ibn Abi Bakr. The lineage runs six generations deep in the naming alone, which is how an Arab family says it has been somebody for a while. He will be called al-Mawsili after the city, al-Taghlabi after the tribe, and once he is grown and known, Taj al-Din, Crown of the Religion. The month comes from the Arabic tradition; the European reference books keep the year and drop it.
stops.quote: ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz Ibn Futūḥ ibn Ibrahīm ibn Abū Bakr, was an Arab writer, mathematician, cryptologist and scribe.
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, 'Ibn al-Durayhim', fetched directly. The Arabic article gives the fourth name as ibn Fath rather than ibn Futuh; the variant is unresolved
suggested_refs: Al-Safadi's biographical notice on Ibn al-Durayhim in A'yan al-'Asr wa-A'wan al-Nasr

stops.name: Mosul, the diminutive of a coin
stops.date_confidence: not an event; the etymology is an undated note in Arabic Wikipedia, placed here at the start of the life for want of anywhere better. Which ancestor carried the nickname is not recorded
stops.campa: The family name is a joke about money, or was one once. Al-Durayhim is the diminutive of dirham, a little silver coin, and it comes down from an ancestor rather than from anything the child does or owns. Nobody records which ancestor, or why. He will carry a small change purse in his name through a life spent on letters, numbers, magic squares and the breaking of ciphers, and the biographers who copy the name out never pause over it. The Arabic notice gives the etymology in a single clause and passes straight on to his teachers.
suggested_refs: Arabic nisba and laqab conventions in Mamluk-era biographical dictionaries

stops.name: Mosul, the Qur'an teacher nobody would otherwise name
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fact, undated in the source; the year is an approximate childhood placement and carries no evidential weight. The teaching site within Mosul is not recorded
stops.campa: The boy learns the Qur'an under Abu Bakr ibn al-Ilm al-Mawsuli, one of the city's Qur'an teachers, a man whose name survives for a single reason: a student of his became famous enough that somebody listed his masters. Where in Mosul the lessons happen is not recorded. What the training gives him is a book held whole in the memory, letter by letter and vowel by vowel, and the habit of hearing written language as a thing made of countable parts. He is eight years old, give or take. No source dates the lesson.
suggested_refs: Qur'anic memorisation and the qira'at curriculum in fourteenth-century Mosul

stops.name: Mosul, law and number from the same voice
stops.date_confidence: attested as a fact, undated in the source; the year is an approximate placement in his youth. The teacher's name is spelled al-Uwayna and al-Uwayya in different renderings of the Arabic notice and is not settled here
stops.campa: He studies Shafi'i jurisprudence and mathematics under one teacher, Zayn al-Din ibn Shaykh al-Uwayna, which looks like an odd pairing now and did not then. Law, arithmetic, astronomy and the properties of letters sit inside a single curriculum and are taught by the same men. A jurist weighing precedent against precedent and a cryptanalyst counting how often a letter recurs are doing recognisably similar work, and in this room they are not even separate subjects. The teacher's name comes down spelled two ways, al-Uwayna and al-Uwayya, and nothing settles which is right.
suggested_refs: The Shafi'i madrasa curriculum and the place of hisab within it

stops.name: Mosul, the road south
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source dates or describes a departure from Mosul. The sources state only that he studied hadith in Egypt at some point, and the journey between the two is entirely undocumented
stops.campa: At some point in his twenties he leaves. No source dates the departure or gives a reason, and no source describes the journey; the record has him in Mosul, and then has him in Egypt studying hadith. It is the road every ambitious scholar of the north takes sooner or later, south and west into the Mamluk lands where the money, the libraries and the appointments are. Ibn Adlan had taken it a century and a half before him. Whether either man ever saw Mosul again is not recorded.
suggested_refs: Scholarly migration from the Jazira to Mamluk Egypt in the fourteenth century

segments.name: Egypt, and a Certificate from a Granadan

stops.name: Cairo, the hadith years
stops.date_confidence: attested that he studied hadith in Egypt; no teacher, no year, no city is named in the sources consulted. Cairo is inferred from where his named grammar teacher taught, and the date is an arbitrary placement
stops.campa: In Egypt he studies hadith, the sourced sayings of the Prophet, the standard leg of any serious Mamluk-era formation. The Arabic biographical tradition states the fact and stops there: no named teacher, no year, no quarter of the city. Cairo in these decades is thick with endowed madrasas and with men exactly like him, provincial, well trained, unplaced. He disappears into it. For these years he is a name with no attached place: the tradition states that he studied hadith in Egypt, and states nothing else about them.
suggested_refs: The hadith madrasas of Mamluk Cairo and their ijaza networks

stops.name: Bayn al-Qasrayn, the ijaza from Abu Hayyan
stops.date_confidence: attested that Abu Hayyan al-Gharnati gave him a formal ijaza in Arabic; the year is nowhere given and is capped only by Abu Hayyan's death in July 1344. The pin is the Qalawun complex on the processional street where Abu Hayyan's teaching circle is placed by inference, not by any source naming a site
stops.campa: Between the two palaces, on the street the Qalawun complex fronts, Ibn al-Durayhim takes an ijaza in Arabic grammar from Athir al-Din Abu Hayyan al-Gharnati. The Granadan has been teaching in Cairo for decades by now, after a youth spent moving through Tunis, Alexandria and Damietta after knowledge. An ijaza is not a diploma issued by an institution. It is one man certifying that another may now teach a text in turn, and what it transmits along with the right is the chain of names it hangs from.
suggested_refs: The ijaza as a transmission instrument in Mamluk scholarship

stops.name: Al-Azhar, taking knowledge from the scholars of Cairo
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the Arabic notice says only that he took knowledge from the scholars of Cairo and names no mosque, no teachers beyond Abu Hayyan, and no years. Al-Azhar is a plausible setting and not an attested one
stops.campa: The circles at al-Azhar and the mosque-schools around it are where a man without a post keeps himself in the conversation: sitting for a lecture, arguing a point, collecting certificates from whoever is worth having one from. He took knowledge from the scholars of Cairo, the notice says of him, and then gives no list. Which mosque, which teachers, which years, none of it survives. Al-Azhar is where such a man would have been. No source puts him there.
suggested_refs: Teaching circles at al-Azhar under the Bahri Mamluks

stops.name: Bab al-Nasr, the grammarian is buried
stops.date_confidence: attested precisely: Abu Hayyan died on Saturday 28 Safar 745 AH / 10 July 1344 after the afternoon prayer, at his house outside Bab al-Bahr, and was buried the following day in the cemetery of the Sufis outside Bab al-Nasr. The pin is placed just north of the gate, where the cemetery lay
stops.campa: Abu Hayyan dies blind in his house outside Bab al-Bahr, on the edge of Cairo, on a Saturday afternoon after the prayer, eighty-seven or eighty-eight years old. They bury him the next day in the cemetery of the Sufis beyond Bab al-Nasr, on the northern side of the walls. The certificate he gave Ibn al-Durayhim is undated, and this funeral is what fixes it: whatever year the ijaza was signed, it was signed before this Saturday, 28 Safar 745. The student is thirty-two, somewhere in the city.
suggested_refs: The Sufi cemetery outside Bab al-Nasr, Cairo

stops.name: Cairo, he reads it aloud
stops.date_confidence: undated tradition reported in Arabic Wikipedia's article on cryptology; no place, no year, no named witness. The claim that he could read ancient Egyptian hieroglyphic inscriptions comes from the same passage and no fourteenth-century scholar could in fact do so
stops.campa: A reputation forms in the scholars' circles and the chancery quarter: hand this man an enciphered letter and he does not retire with it. He converts it as he reads and speaks the plain Arabic aloud, on sight, the way another man reads a page of ordinary prose. The account is undated and names no witness. The same passage credits him with reading the old picture writing on the monuments upriver, which nobody in his century can actually do, and reputations for deciphering attract that kind of addition.
suggested_refs: Arabic accounts of hieroglyphic decipherment before Champollion

stops.name: Cairo, the key to the treasures
stops.date_confidence: no composition date survives; the year is a mid-career placement only. The title is unsettled: the Arabic list gives Miftah al-kunuz fi idah al-marmuz, English-language cataloguing gives Maqasid al-fusul al-mutarjama an hall al-tarjama, and no source consulted states whether these are one work or two. Place of composition is unrecorded
stops.campa: He writes the cipher book. In the Arabic list of his works it stands as Miftah al-kunuz fi idah al-marmuz, Key to the Treasures on Clarifying the Encoded; in the English-language catalogues it stands as Maqasid al-fusul al-mutarjama an hall al-tarjama, Clear Chapters Goals and Solving Ciphers. Whether these are two names for one book or two books, the sources do not settle. Inside it the method of al-Kindi and of Ibn Adlan is not merely used but organised: cipher types set out as a system, worked examples, tables of letter frequencies.
stops.quote: Also traced to Ibn al-Durayhim is an exposition on and a worked example of cryptanalysis, including the use of tables of letter frequencies and sets of letters which cannot occur together in one word.
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, 'History of cryptography', fetched directly
suggested_refs: The competing titles of Ibn al-Durayhim's cryptology treatise

stops.name: Cairo, the table two centuries early
stops.date_confidence: attested that the treatise contains the earliest known suggestion of a tableau of the kind later called the Vigenere table; undated. One verification pass reported that the figure of eight cipher systems does not appear in the English Wikipedia article, while a direct quotation pass reproduced the sentence containing it verbatim from that same article. The contradiction is left open
stops.campa: Among the systems he describes is an arrangement of the alphabet against itself, a grid whose rows shift, so that one plaintext letter can stand for several different ciphertext letters depending on where in the message it falls. Frequency counting, the weapon he inherited, does not bite well against it. He gives the arrangement no name of its own and does not treat it as the centre of his book. Two hundred years later Blaise de Vigenere publishes the same idea, and the table is called his.
stops.quote: gave detailed descriptions of eight cipher systems that discussed substitution ciphers, leading to the earliest suggestion of a 'tableau' of the kind that two centuries later became known as the 'Vigenère table'
suggested_refs: The polyalphabetic tableau before Blaise de Vigenère

stops.name: Cairo, the ciphers put into verse
stops.date_confidence: attested that he composed a long didactic qasida on methods of enciphering; undated, unplaced, and no line of it is quoted in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He also puts it into verse. A long didactic qasida sets out methods of enciphering in meter and rhyme. Verse in Arabic is a delivery system: a poem is portable, a student carries it across a desert in his head, a treatise stays on a shelf in one city. Medicine, grammar, law and arithmetic are all taught this way, in lines a student memorises before he understands them, for centuries. The poem is undated, and the sources consulted quote not a line of it. It is one entry in a list of two dozen titles.
suggested_refs: Didactic qasida as a teaching form in the Arabic sciences

stops.name: Mosul, the shape of a working life
stops.date_confidence: the corpus of roughly two dozen works is an aggregate with no internal dating; the pin is symbolic, since not one of these titles has a recorded place of composition. Different summaries of the same Arabic source give 24, 25 and 27 as the total, and the lowest figure is used here
stops.campa: The list of his books runs to roughly two dozen and refuses to stay inside a subject. A commentary on an arithmetic text. Studies of magic squares, those grids in which every row and column and diagonal come to the same sum. A treatise on chess. Essays on the numerical values hidden in the ninety-nine names of God. Physiognomy, etymology, divination, the meanings of Islamic names. Al-Safadi's notice runs them together as one appetite. Not a title on the list carries a recorded date or a recorded place of composition.
suggested_refs: The bibliographic list of Ibn al-Durayhim's works in the Arabic biographical tradition

stops.name: Damascus, half a conversation in riddles
stops.date_confidence: attested that the exchange took place and that Ibn al-Durayhim wrote it up; undated. Damascus is inferred from al-Safadi's documented residence there as katib al-sirr, not stated in the source as the site of the exchange
stops.campa: He and Salah al-Din al-Safadi, secretary of the bureau in Damascus and the most industrious biographer of the age, carry on an exchange of riddles and technical enigmas, each setting the other problems in the disguising and unpicking of words. Ibn al-Durayhim writes his side up as al-Muhawara al-Salahiyya fi al-Ahjahi al-Istilahiyya. Al-Safadi writes his own version, Najm al-Diyaji fi Nazm al-Ahjahi, and it is lost. What survives is a single copy at the Escorial, shelved as manuscript 432, half of a conversation.
suggested_refs: Escorial Arabic manuscript 432, al-Muhawara al-Salahiyya

segments.name: The Animals, and the Boy in the Delta

stops.name: Cairo, the usefulness of animals
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1355 by English Wikipedia, one of the few firm dates in his life. The place of composition is not recorded and Cairo is inferred from his years there; no source consulted supports a dedication to any Mamluk sultan
stops.campa: He compiles Manafi' al-Hayawan, the Book on the Usefulness of Animals: what each creature is good for, in medicine, in the household, against the ailments the physicians name. He works from the Christian court physician Ibn Bakhtishu' and from Aristotle, whose zoology came into Arabic through the translators of Baghdad four centuries earlier and has been compiled and recompiled ever since. Whether he writes it in Cairo or somewhere else the record does not say. The year is one of the very few fixed points in his life.
suggested_refs: The Ibn Bakhtishu' tradition of Manafi' al-Hayawan manuscripts

stops.name: Cairo, ninety-one creatures painted in
stops.date_confidence: attested that the surviving Escorial copy contains 91 animal illustrations; whether the illustrations belong to the original compilation or to the surviving copy is not stated in the sources consulted, and the month here is an ordering device only
stops.campa: The copy that survives is illustrated: ninety-one animals painted into the text, one after another, a bestiary carried inside a manual. The pictures are what make the manuscript valuable to collectors, and eventually what make it travel. A cipher treatise is a working tool, used until it falls apart or shelved until nobody knows what it is. An illustrated animal book is an object, and objects get bought, inventoried, packed and shipped. Lions, hares, birds of prey, snakes, each with its uses set down beside its picture.
suggested_refs: Escorial Arabic manuscript 898 and its ninety-one animal miniatures

stops.name: Qalqashanda, a boy born in the delta
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1355 or 1356 by English Wikipedia; the two years are not adjudicated. The pin is the approximate centre of the village of Qalqashanda in Qalyubia and not a documented house
stops.campa: In a village in the Nile Delta, in what is now Qalyubia, a boy is born to a family that gives him the village's name: Ahmad ibn Ali al-Qalqashandi. Nearly everything anyone will ever read of Ibn al-Durayhim's cipher work is going to pass through this child's handwriting, in a reference book he finishes fifty-six years from now. He is five or six when Ibn al-Durayhim dies, and the two never meet and never correspond. The reference works give his birth as 1355 or 1356 and do not choose between them.
suggested_refs: Qalqashanda, Qalyubia governorate, birthplace of al-Qalqashandi

stops.name: Unrecorded ground, the year 762
stops.date_confidence: the death year is contested. Arabic Wikipedia gives 762 AH, which runs from 11 November 1360 to 30 October 1361, so the Hijri year maps to 1360/1361 and not flatly to 1361; English Wikipedia gives a range of 1359 to 1362. No source consulted names a city of death or a burial place, and this pin is a placeholder at the last milieu he is attested in, not a claim about where he died
stops.campa: He dies in the year 762 of the Hijra, forty-eight or forty-nine years old. The Hijri year straddles two Christian ones, running from November 1360 into October 1361, and the English reference books give a range of 1359 to 1362 instead, so the date is soft on both sides. No source consulted names the city. No source names a grave, a mosque, a quarter, or a month. Mosul raised him and Egypt seems to have held most of his working life, and the record stops without choosing between them.
suggested_refs: Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, for Mamluk-era obituaries not reached in this pass

stops.name: Damascus, a wonder of his time
stops.date_confidence: the notice is undated; al-Safadi died in July 1363, which caps it. The Arabic Wikipedia article's own footnote attributes the sentence to al-Safadi's A'yan al-'Asr wa-A'wan al-Nasr, iii.523-24, not to al-Wafi bi'l-Wafayat as several summaries state. Neither printed edition was checked directly
stops.campa: In Damascus, Khalil ibn Aybak al-Safadi, katib al-sirr and keeper of the treasury, writes his correspondent into the biographical dictionaries he has been filling for thirty years. He will be dead within two years himself. The entry is short. It names cryptography, the properties of letters, magic squares and riddles, and then jurisprudence, hadith and the roots of religion. It opens: he was a wonder among the wonders of the age in his intelligence.
stops.quote: كان أعجوبة من أعاجيب الزمان في ذكائه
stops.quote_source: al-Safadi, A'yan al-'Asr wa-A'wan al-Nasr, iii.523-24, as quoted in Arabic Wikipedia, 'ابن الدريهم' (raw wikitext fetched directly); English sense: 'he was a wonder among the wonders of the age in his intelligence'. Not checked against a printed edition
suggested_refs: Al-Safadi, A'yan al-'Asr wa-A'wan al-Nasr, volume iii

stops.name: Damascus, the biographer dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; al-Safadi (born 696 AH / 1296, not 1297 as several summaries give) died at Damascus on 23 July 1363
stops.campa: Al-Safadi dies in Damascus on the twenty-third of July, 1363. He leaves al-Wafi bi'l-Wafayat, which runs to some thirty volumes in its modern printed edition, and A'yan al-'Asr beside it, and in passing the only near-contemporary description anyone has of Ibn al-Durayhim's mind. Chancery officials who wrote biographies are the reason certain fourteenth-century people can be described at all. Neither of his books has been read here in a printed edition; the sentence about Ibn al-Durayhim comes down through a transcription of a transcription.
suggested_refs: Al-Wafi bi'l-Wafayat, the largest biographical dictionary of the Mamluk period

stops.name: The Citadel, the Diwan al-Insha
stops.date_confidence: attested that al-Qalqashandi served in the Mamluk chancery as katib al-darj, Scribe of the Scroll; the year here is an arbitrary placement inside a career the sources do not date year by year
stops.campa: Al-Qalqashandi builds his career inside the Diwan al-Insha, the chancery of correspondence, up in the Citadel on the spur of the Muqattam. The office requires knowing, among a hundred other technical matters, how a cipher is put together and how it comes apart, because a chancery that cannot read its enemies' mail is not a chancery, and that requirement is what sends him looking for the Mosuli's book. The daily work is drafting: the sultan's letters, treaties and appointments, in a rule-bound ornamental prose that takes years to learn.
suggested_refs: The Diwan al-Insha in the Cairo Citadel and the office of katib al-darj

stops.name: Cairo, the method enters the manual
stops.date_confidence: attested; Subh al-a'sha, in fourteen volumes, was completed in 1412. That its cryptology section quotes Ibn al-Durayhim is attested; the claim in circulation that it does so nearly verbatim, and the volume and section numbers sometimes cited for it, could not be verified against the text
stops.campa: He finishes Subh al-a'sha fi Sina'at al-Insha, fourteen volumes on everything a government secretary needs: geography, political history, natural history, minerals, cosmography, and the mechanics of the office itself. One section handles secret correspondence, and that section is Ibn al-Durayhim's, quoted from a treatise fifty years old and already hard to come by. Frequency analysis becomes an entry in a manual that clerks pull off a shelf at their desks. How much of the treatise he copies, and from which copy, cannot be checked here: the text of Subh al-a'sha was not retrieved, and no volume or section is cited.
stops.quote: The work of Al-Qalqashandi (1355-1418), based on the earlier work of Ibn al-Durayhim (1312-1359), contained the first published discussion of the substitution and transposition of ciphers, as well as the first description of a polyalphabetic cipher, in which each plaintext letter is assigned more than one substitute.
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, 'Substitution cipher', fetched directly, summarising David Kahn
sources: David Kahn, The Codebreakers (via secondary quotation)
suggested_refs: Subh al-a'sha fi Sina'at al-Insha, completed 1412, and its section on secret correspondence

stops.name: Cairo, the scribe dies and the copy holds
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1418; no day or month recorded in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Al-Qalqashandi dies in Cairo at sixty-two or sixty-three, in the city where he spent his working life inside one office. What becomes of Ibn al-Durayhim's own treatise after this is not recorded in anything reached for this account. Subh al-a'sha outlives the Mamluk state it was written to serve, and so does the passage inside it that quotes a dead man's cipher book. Clerks need the encyclopedia, so the encyclopedia gets copied, and copied again.
stops.quote: Al-Qalqashandi quoted the text relevant to cryptology from the work of Ibn al-Durayhim (1312–1361) that was once considered lost.
suggested_refs: The manuscript and print transmission of Subh al-a'sha

stops.name: El Escorial, Arabic manuscript 898
stops.date_confidence: the manuscript's presence at the Escorial as Ar. 898 is attested; its route there is not. The 1614 date is the documented incorporation of the captured Saadian library of Sultan Zidan, offered as the likeliest occasion and nothing more. No source consulted links the two
stops.campa: The animal book ends up in a monastery library in the sierra northwest of Madrid, catalogued as Arabic manuscript 898. How it got there is in no source consulted: not the hands it passed through, not the port it left from, not the century. Spanish ships took the library of the Saadian sultan Zidan at sea in 1612 and the books were carried up to the Escorial two years later, the largest single arrival of Arabic manuscripts in Christian Spain. That is the likeliest occasion and nothing more. Nobody has established it.
sources: maslama_al_qurtubi.journey.json, for the Zidan library capture and its 1614 incorporation
suggested_refs: The Arabic manuscripts of the Real Biblioteca del Monasterio de El Escorial

stops.name: Cairo, the verdict of lost
stops.date_confidence: not an event; the date marks the long pre-rediscovery consensus in European and English-language scholarship, which cannot be pinned to a year. The judgment is still repeated in reference works that also report the treatise found
stops.campa: For most of the modern period the verdict on the cipher treatise is simple: gone. Historians of cryptography writing in English work from al-Qalqashandi's quotation and say so plainly, that the writings on cryptography of the man they are quoting are lost. He exists as a citation inside another man's encyclopedia. What he actually wrote, at what length, in what order, and what he thought he was doing, cannot be recovered from a chapter of extracts. How much of the book that chapter represents, none of this literature says.
stops.quote: This information was attributed to Ibn al-Durayhim who lived from AD 1312 to 1361, but whose writings on cryptography have been lost.
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, 'History of cryptography', fetched directly
suggested_refs: David Kahn, The Codebreakers (1967), on the Arab cryptological tradition

stops.name: Istanbul, the Risala comes back into print
stops.date_confidence: attested that al-Kadi's 'Origins of Cryptology: The Arab Contributions' appeared in Cryptologia 16:2 (1992); the article itself could not be retrieved this session (ResearchGate returned 403). The Suleymaniye recovery in Istanbul is attested for al-Kindi's works only. English Wikipedia says of Ibn al-Durayhim's treatise only that it was recently discovered and unpublished, and names no repository. Sources that place his treatise in the same Istanbul archive are merging two separate stories, and the merger is flagged, not resolved
stops.campa: Ibrahim al-Kadi publishes 'Origins of Cryptology: The Arab Contributions' in Cryptologia and the chain becomes visible to a modern audience: al-Kindi, Ibn Adlan, Ibn al-Durayhim, al-Qalqashandi, four centuries of work on breaking ciphers that European histories had begun with the Renaissance. Al-Kindi's own Risala is recovered from the Ottoman archives in Istanbul, catalogued and unread for four hundred years. What happened to Ibn al-Durayhim's treatise is told differently in different places, and the accounts do not agree.
stops.quote: His book titled Clear Chapters Goals and Solving Ciphers was recently discovered, but has yet to be published. It includes the use of the statistical techniques pioneered by Al-Kindi and Ibn 'Adlan.
sources: Ibrahim A. Al-Kadi, Cryptologia 16:2 (1992) (via secondary quotation)
suggested_refs: Ibrahim A. Al-Kadi, 'Origins of Cryptology: The Arab Contributions', Cryptologia 16:2 (1992)

stops.name: Riyadh, the series nobody in this account could open
stops.date_confidence: unverified. The Series on Arabic Origins of Cryptology, associated with M. Mrayati, Y. Meer Alam and M. H. al-Tayyan and published through the King Faisal Center for Research and Islamic Studies, is reported to edit and translate Ibn al-Durayhim's cryptological material, but the volumes and the publisher pages could not be reached this session, so neither the contents nor the years are confirmed. The pin is the city, not the building
stops.campa: A multi-volume critical edition of the Arabic cryptological manuscripts is prepared by M. Mrayati, Y. Meer Alam and M. H. al-Tayyan, published through the King Faisal Center in Riyadh and, in part, in English translation, and it is in this series that specialists say Ibn al-Durayhim's own text is edited at last. The volumes could not be reached to check what they contain or when precisely they appeared. Everything said here about the treatise's modern fate rests on other people's citations of them.

stops.name: Mosul, no grave and no legend
stops.date_confidence: not an event; a statement of the record's condition. No tomb, shrine, marker, ziyara tradition, miracle story or popular legend for Ibn al-Durayhim was found in any source consulted, and absence of evidence in accessible sources is not proof that none exists in the archives not reached
stops.campa: There is no tomb, no shrine, no marker. No pilgrimage develops, no miracle story attaches, no legend grows in the mouths of a city that produced two of the four men in this line. His readers are specialists, in the fifteenth century and again in the twentieth, and nothing in any source consulted suggests he was remembered outside them. What survives is text: an animal book in Spain, half a riddle-dialogue in the same library, a cipher treatise reported found and still not printed, and a chapter in somebody else's encyclopedia.
sources: Absence across all sources consulted: Arabic Wikipedia, English Wikipedia, secondary cryptology-history literature
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of al-Nuri, Mosul, and the city's Mamluk-era scholarly output
